question: A 3-year-old child presents with classic measles with high fever, the 3 C's prodrome, Koplik spots, and a cephalocaudal maculopapular rash. He is malnourished (weight-for-height Z-score −2.5). Which of the following specific interventions reduces measles-related mortality and complications including blindness in this child?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Oseltamivir targets influenza neuraminidase and has no role in measles treatment. There is no licensed antiviral for measles.

answers.text: High-dose Vitamin A supplementation (200,000 IU for children over 1 year) given on 2 consecutive days

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. WHO and IAP recommend Vitamin A supplementation for ALL children with measles, regardless of nutritional status. In malnourished children and those in developing countries, Vitamin A reduces measles mortality by 50% and prevents xerophthalmia/corneal ulceration causing blindness. Dose: 200,000 IU on days 1 and 2 for children over 1 year; 100,000 IU for 6–12 month olds.

answers.text: Prophylactic antibiotics to prevent secondary bacterial infections

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Antibiotics are given therapeutically if secondary bacterial pneumonia or otitis media develops — not routinely as prophylaxis for all measles cases.

answers.text: Intravenous gamma-globulin infusion to neutralise the virus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. IVIG can be used for post-exposure prophylaxis in immunocompromised contacts within 6 days of exposure, but not as treatment for active measles.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the measles management section. The key specific intervention is Vitamin A supplementation — 200,000 IU for 2 consecutive days (children >1 year). This reduces mortality by ~50% and prevents measles-related blindness.

Correct. High-dose Vitamin A (200,000 IU for 2 days in children over 1 year) is a proven, evidence-based intervention that reduces measles mortality and prevents blindness, especially in malnourished children.
